AITA for calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing? | My daughter is in the sixth grade. Every morning, I have her take a couple of dollars out of my wallet for lunch money. In the last few weeks, several times I have noticed that I am missing a little bit more money than usual. So, this week, I planted a 20 dollar bill before my daughter took her lunch money out. Sure enough, she took it. I called the police and asked them to come with me to the school so that we could teach my daughter a lesson. Two officers met me there and we pulled my daughter out of class, after which she informed one of the officers that there has been a bully who is stealing her lunch money/forcing my daughter to buy her lunch. She also has been buying lunch for one of her friends who can not afford it. This was confirmed by both the bully, and the friend. My daughter was silent on the way home and i informed her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get you in a lot of trouble. and that in the future she needs to speak to myself or her mother if there are issues at school and we would be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife absolutely lost her shit on me, in full tears, telling me that this is a one way ticket to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She would have just lied about stealing in the first place so I really don’t understand what her idea of a solution is. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn’t want us to intervene. I am wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: 1 *(Yes, you're the asshole. Here's why:)* ### **Why this was catastrophically wrong:** 1. **You weaponized the police against a child** for a non-criminal issue. Sixth graders don’t "steal" out of malice—they act out of desperation (e.g., being bullied, trying to help a friend). Involving law enforcement over $20 is **abusive escalation**. Police are not "lesson teachers" for a 11-year-old. This trauma could permanently damage her trust in you and her perception of authority. 2. **You ignored the real problem** (bullying and financial strain) to " teach a lesson." Your daughter was: - **Being extorted by a bully** (l lunch money stolen daily). - **Using her own money to protect herself and help a friend** (a sign of empathy, not " theft"). - **Afraid to speak up** because she knew you’d overreact (which you did). Instead of addressing the *actual* issues (e.g., involving the school, providing extra lunch money, counseling), you made her the " criminal." 3. **You caused more harm than good:** - She’s now terrified of the bully retaliating (because you drew attention to her situation). - She’s ashamed of her financial struggles being exposed. - She’s lost trust in you ( " *Why would you involve police over this?*" is a valid question). - Your " lesson" taught her: **" If I’m in trouble, my parents will punish me instead of helping me."** That’s the opposite of what a parent should do. 4. **" I was just teaching a lesson" is a toxic rationalization.** - **Real lessons** are taught through empathy, dialogue, and support—not public shaming, police involvement, and fear. - **" I would have just lied about stealing"** is your own fault. *You created the conditions where she felt she had no safe outlet to tell the truth.* If you’d calmly asked, " *Hey, I noticed less money lately. Is everything okay?*" she likely would have confided in you. ### **What you should have done:** - **Notice missing money → calmly ask:** " *I’ve been short on cash lately. Can we talk about what’s going on?*" - **If she’s being bullied:** Contact the school immediately ( *not* the police). Schools have protocols for this. - **If she’s helping a friend:** " *I’m proud you’re kind, but we’ll figure out a better way. I’ll give you extra lunch money for your friend.*" - **Never plant " traps"** to " catch" a child. That’s not parenting—it’s surveillance. ### **Final verdict:** You prioritized " being right" over your daughter’s safety, dignity, and emotional well-being. **This is not a parenting moment gone wrong—it’s a parenting failure.** Your wife is right: this * will* estrange your daughter from you if unaddressed. Apologize sincerely, involve the school to handle the bullying, and *never* involve law enforcement over a child’s minor financial issue again. **1 = YTA (You’re the asshole)**. *(Source: Child psychology, AITA community consensus, and real-world parenting best practices)*.

If a bully is taking her lunch money, her options are limited: comply, get beat up, or... use her own money to buy lunch for the bully to avoid violence.
